description: Solo participant from Hanoi, Vietnam, joining the Hanoi Local Event virtually. I'm an Electronics & Telecommunications student at Hanoi University of Science and Technology (HUST), interested in AI, data, and building practical web applications. Looking forward to exploring NASA data and turning it into something useful in 48 hours.
summary:
EarthPulse is a free web app that turns high-school and college students into data detectives. A student who plots one NASA variable and sees a line going up cannot tell a real trend from noise, or from a jump in the data itself. EarthPulse tests every 1° land cell for 11 NASA variables over 2001–2024: seven land variables from GLDAS and GPM IMERG, and four atmosphere variables from MERRA-2. It then cross-examines each result: Is it significant? Could it be a data glitch? Does a second NASA dataset agree?

It addresses the challenge directly: it selects variables, shows how they change over time, and says what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is significant. In one minute a student picks a place (for example Vietnam) and a question (for example Heat) and reads a plain-language answer with the rate of change, a 95% interval, a warning if the series jumps, and whether a second dataset agrees. Example: 58.5% of land shows a significant rise in near-surface air temperature, but 48.8% of the significant area carries a sudden-shift flag.

It matters because a headline trend can be a real change or a glitch in the data. Students who learn to ask how sure we are can read any climate claim better. EarthPulse adds a report for each of 143 countries, a one-page classroom sheet in English and Vietnamese, and plain definitions of every term.
details:
What it does

EarthPulse is a free web app for high-school and college students that tests whether trends in NASA Earth data are real. A student picks a place and a question, and gets a plain-language answer for each NASA variable. Every trend is then cross-examined with three questions: Is the change statistically significant? Could it be a glitch in the data? Does a second NASA dataset agree? The app gives a plain verdict, for example "read with caution", and keeps the evidence one click away.

It covers 11 variables over 2001–2024 on a 1° land grid: surface and air temperature, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, specific humidity and rainfall, plus four atmosphere variables (air temperature at 850 and 500 hPa, column water vapour and total ozone). Every one of 143 countries has its own report, and the whole app works in English and Vietnamese.

The problem it solves

A line that goes up on a chart is not an answer. It may be noise: testing thousands of places at once at p < 0.05 produces many false alarms. It may be a jump in the data itself: one of the products we use, GLDAS-2.1, is documented as not fully homogeneous over time, and a step can look like a trend. And one dataset is only one opinion.

How it works

Monthly NASA files (GLDAS Noah 2.1, GPM IMERG V07 and MERRA-2) are put on a common 1° grid and turned into anomalies, so the seasonal cycle is removed. For every cell, variable and period, a Python pipeline computes the rate of change (Sen's slope), tests it with the Hamed–Rao modified Mann–Kendall test, which allows for month-to-month dependence, and controls false discoveries across all cells (Benjamini–Hochberg, q < 0.05). A change-point test flags cells where the series jumps instead of rising steadily. The same test is run on a second NASA product (MERRA-2, or GPCP for rainfall) to see whether it agrees. The web app reads the validated results; no language model produces any number.

Example: Vietnam. Air temperature rises +0.43 °C per decade (95% interval +0.22 to +0.63), which is significant. But 54% of the country's area shows a sudden shift around 2012, and the second dataset, MERRA-2, gives only +0.07 °C per decade, not significant. The verdict is "read with caution": warming in both datasets, direction agreed, size uncertain.

Why the cross-examination matters: for air temperature, a simple test marks 78.0% of land as significant; our method marks 62.5%. Worldwide, 58.5% of land warms significantly, but 48.8% of that area shows a sudden shift.

Pages: Investigate (three short questions: where, what, which years), Variables (all variables ranked), Map (trends, data-quality flags and agreement on one map), Cases (five worked examples), the country case file (chart, interval, significance, second dataset, CSV download, and links to re-run the check in NASA Giovanni), and How it works.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve

For students, EarthPulse turns "the line goes up" into three better questions and an answer in about a minute. For teachers, it gives a report for each of 143 countries and a one-page classroom sheet. We hope students build one habit: ask "how sure are we?" before repeating a headline, and learn that a significant trend is evidence, not proof of cause, and that two datasets that disagree are a finding, not a failure. Our next step is to try it with a real class.

How it is creative

Most trend tools stop at "significant or not". EarthPulse treats every trend like a witness in a court case: it is questioned three times, and the answer is a verdict with its uncertainty, not just a coloured map. It shows openly where NASA datasets disagree, such as specific humidity, where the second dataset contradicts 39.3% of the significant area.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty first: every number comes with its uncertainty, "not significant" is never shown as "no change", and a data-quality flag is a warning, not proof of error. We state our limits: land only, 1° resolution, monthly data, linear trends, and both GLDAS and MERRA-2 are models, not ground truth. We also made it easy to use: no installation, no account, plain definitions for every term, phone-friendly pages and an English/Vietnamese switch.

Tools and languages

Python (NumPy, pandas, xarray, netCDF4, SciPy, statsmodels, pymannkendall, earthaccess) for the data pipeline; TypeScript, React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Plotly.js and three.js for the web app; Vitest and Playwright for testing. Open source under Apache-2.0.

Development timeline

The data pipeline, the statistics and the first version of the app were built before the event, on 9–10 Nov 2026, with more interface work from 10 to 13 Nov. During the event (14–15 Nov) we changed the regional test to the Hamed–Rao method, compared it with the simple method, added the four atmosphere variables, built the new interface (3D globe, case file, verdict map, country report, classroom sheet, check-it-yourself links) and the English/Vietnamese switch. The commit history at https://github.com/imninh/EarthPusle_NS is the record.
